Witness statement of DR DAPHNE CHONG (read)
May I read two statements, please? Firstly, from a Daphne Chong, whose statement is at page 8 of your Lordship's reading bundle.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Members of the jury, Dr Chong made a statement dated 17 May 2018. The relevant parts of which I read to you, beginning with:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "At the time of the birth of [Baby J], I was an ST5 working in the Countess of Chester Hospital."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Under the title "Birth of [Baby J]":
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I have reviewed the maternity notes of this birth and can comment as below.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On 30 October 2015, [Mother of Baby J], [Baby J]'s mum, had been admitted by the day unit team. She had been known to have a premature rupture of the membrane (waters broken) with her pregnancy, which was currently at 32 weeks.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Mother of Baby J]’s membrane had ruptured on 7 October 2015 and she had been having outpatient monitoring. She was admitted on 30 October 2015 as there had been a change from an outpatient monitoring point of view which was suggesting infection.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Her pregnancy had initially been a twin pregnancy with a condition that was compromising the pregnancy early on, known as twin-to-twin transfusion, with one of the twins dying prenatally.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "On 31 October 2015, I was working a 12-hour shift at the Countess of Chester Hospital. At approximately 09.30 hours I was completing ward rounds with Dr Davies and examined [Mother of Baby J] and felt that the complication from the ruptured membrane was becoming infected.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "When the membranes have ruptured during pregnancy, there are two main risks which are prematurity and infection. The liquid that [Mother of Baby J] was passing had changed and she was having stomachaches. In this case the risk of infection
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: outweighed of that prematurity and I made the decision that the caesarean operation for [Mother of Baby J] should be brought forward to later that day.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I completed the caesarean section with no complications and [Baby J] was handed to the midwife with my notes stating:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "'Straightforward entry. Delivery with blood loss of 300ml.'
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I then continued to care for [Mother of Baby J]. The placenta was delivered with no complications and was removed at the same time as the caesarean section. I closed [Mother of Baby J]’s abdomen and she went to recovery whilst I left the theatre.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "If there were any complications during birth I would see the patient the same day. Because [Mother of Baby J]’s caesarean section was completed with no complications, I saw her on the post-natal ward the next day when she was wanting to be discharged as [Baby J] had been taken to Alder Hey Children's Hospital and she wanted to be with her. [Mother of Baby J] was discharged that day."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Witness statement of DR SARAH WOOD (read)
The next statement to be read is from Sarah Wood, whose statement is at page 23. A statement dated, members of the jury, 16 April 2020, stating:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "I am employed as a consultant paediatric and neonatal surgeon at Alder Hey Children's National Health Service Foundation Trust.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "My role is a general paediatric surgeon covering elective and emergency cases in both children and neonates. As a hospital, we also provide outreach services to Chester.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby J], date of birth 31 October 2015, was referred on 31 October 2015 by Chester hospital with bilious vomiting and radiology consistent with possible bowel obstruction and possible compromised bowel (malrotation/volvulus). This was on the background of being premature, that is to say 32 weeks and 2 days, and the surviving twin of twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome. On transfer to Alder Hey on 1 November 2015, she was intubated and ventilated, on antibiotics, with appropriate intravenous access. The transfer was to the paediatric intensive care unit.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby J] was taken to theatre by myself as an emergency with the finding of intra-abdominal adhesions and an isolated dilated loop of small bowel with an intestinal perforation. We resected
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: this perforated bowel (7.5 centimetres) and formed stomas. We also inserted a tunnelled central line for nutrition (Broviac)."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So that's the nature of a Broviac line and shortly, my Lord, the jury will watch an animation of a Broviac line:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Pathology from this procedure was consistent with necrotising enterocolitis (bowel death), a condition seen in premature infants or those with a restriction of blood flow to the bowel.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby J] recovered well post-operatively. In the notes of 9 November 2015 made by a colleague, Dr Shaw, a consultant neonatologist, it is commented that she could be transferred back to Chester for ongoing management. This was noted again on 10 November 2015 and transfer back was arranged with a plan for stoma closures in January 2016.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Feeds were being increased at 2ml eight-hourly with a concurrent reduction in intravenous feed TPN.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "She was having her stoma output recycled. There is documentation on 9 November to suggest that Chester confirmed they were able to perform the recycling. Her central line remained in situ as she was still having feeds through this.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Cardiology were planning, at discharge, to review her echo images and inform Chester of her planned follow-up."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: This witness's statement then moves forward in time to 23 December 2015, which corresponds to an entry at tile 356 on our sequence of events. If Mr Murphy could put that up so we can all orientate ourselves.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: This is a point in time when [Baby J] had returned to Chester, then been moved to Manchester, and was discharged from Manchester back to Alder Hey.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Returning to the statement:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "[Baby J] was transferred back to Alder Hey under my care on 23 December 2015 from Royal Manchester Children's Hospital. She was recovering from a Klebsiella line infection, which had been treated in Manchester due to lack of beds in Alder Hey. This infection grew from a culture from her tunnelled central line, the Broviac line. She recovered as expected.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The plan for stoma closures altered due to her inpatient status along with some complications with a fistula, which is an extra opening at the base, causing leakage ++.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "This had meant that it was challenging to recycle the stoma output into her other downstream stoma, which meant her weight had faltered. Her weight had dropped from the 50th centile to under the 0.4 by readmission. The date for the stoma closures was therefore brought forward to 30 December 2015.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "The stoma closure on 31 December 2015 (performed by myself) was straightforward and [Baby J] was discharged fully fed on 6 January 2016.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Her tunnelled central line (Broviac line) was removed by Mr Robert Peters, a registrar, on 5 January 2016 before discharge.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Clinical reviews in Alder Hey on 12 February 2016, 15 March 2016 and 19 May 2017 in outpatients were as expected. She initially had some blood in her stools, but this was felt to be secondary to milk allergy. This settled with cows' milk protein exclusion as recommended by an Alder Hey dietician.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

DR JOHN GIBBS (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR DRIVER
Dr Gibbs, could you state your full name for the transcript, please?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm John Gibbs.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Dr Gibbs, as I am sure your appreciate, you have been invited back this morning to provide evidence in relation to [Baby J], who was born at the Countess of Chester Hospital on 31 October 2015.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: In preparation for your re-attendance at this trial, have you reminded yourself of the relevant parts of the clinical notes that were written up about [Baby J] during her time at Chester?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Are you appraised of the antenatal history?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And are you appraised of the circumstances immediately before and of [Baby J]'s birth?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: She was born at 32 weeks and 2 days' gestation, we understand. Have you reminded yourself of the treatment that she received in the first few hours of life?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, I have.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What was the extent of the support that she required in the very first moments of her life?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I think briefly, [Baby J] needed some help with her breathing, as expected as 32 weeks, but the main problem was that she was producing bile out of her nasogastric tube and also spontaneously bringing up/regurgitating bile.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Based on your experience, what are those symptoms indicative of?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, if there is a reasonable amount, a repeated amount of bile, there may be an obstruction in the bowel.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Do the notes record that at 5 hours of age the nursing staff noted that bile was obtained from aspirating the nasogastric tube?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And did that continue over the next few hours?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And hence was she examined by registrar paediatric doctors?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. I wasn't involved at that time, but I've read -- I knew about that history and I've reminded myself from the notes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What was discovered and what were the consequences of those discoveries?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, an abdominal X-ray showed an unusual bowel gas pattern and [Baby J] was discussed with the surgeons at the Alder Hey Hospital in Liverpool and it was felt that the combination of features she was showing might indicate a bowel problem, there may be a bowel blockage, and the plan was for her to be transferred to Liverpool.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: For that reason, she was electively planned to be ventilated to keep her stable to be transferred to Alder Hey Hospital.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So expand upon that. Was she sedated pre-transport?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I believe so, yes. That would normally be the case when electively intubating a baby, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And intubated so as to enable mechanical ventilation, if required?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If we just, with Mr Murphy's assistance, please, go to tile 6 to remind ourselves of the chronology.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Born at 15.00 hours on 31 October and tile 6 indicates a transfer at or around 04.00 hours on 1 November, that is to say within the first 24 hours of her life.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We know that she eventually returned to the Countess of Chester Hospital, but before doing so, did she undergo abdominal surgery at Alder Hey?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, she did.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What was the nature of her problem and what was done to address that problem?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, I believe the surgeons found a perforation, a hole, in part of the small bowel, towards the lower end of the small bowel, which is called the ileum, and there were a lot of adhesions, meaning strands of fibrous tissue, sticking the bowel together, which would suggest that that perforation had happened some time before. I'm not able to say exactly how long before, but I would have thought days or more before. So it may have happened before she was born, but not recognised until after she was born.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Was that consistent with the antenatal history particular to [Baby J]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, it is a complication. Bowel disturbances are a complication of twin-to-twin transfusion, the problems that affected [Baby J] and her, sadly, deceased twin.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What about the treatment that was provided to the twins and [Baby J]'s mother because of the twin-to-twin transfusion?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, to try and prevent the swapping of blood between the two twins inside the womb, some of the blood vessels in the placenta connecting the two twin's placentas together with divided by laser. It is reported that that laser treatment can sometimes cause blood clots that can settle out in the bowel. But just having twin-to-twin transfusion can overload one twin and underload, take blood away, from the other twin and that can damage either twin's bowel.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So the problem discovered and addressed at Alder Hey by one route or another may very well have been the consequence of the twin-to-twin transfusion?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. What was the surgical intervention? What did they do at Alder Hey?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The surgeons had to remove part of [Baby J]'s bowel, so that's part of her ileum. And looking at the surgical note, because I wasn't involved in that surgery at all, it was a difficult surgery. So they had to extend the abdominal wound for [Baby J], giving her quite a wide incision across her upper abdomen in order to divide the adhesions and try and free the bowel. And they had to create two stomas. I don't know if stomas have been explained to the court.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Right. Because part of the bowel had been damaged and the surgeons didn't want to just put the bowel back together again because it may well break down when [Baby J] started to feed, they had to remove the damaged part of the bowel. The bit of bowel above it was brought through the surface of the abdominal wall to create a little opening in the abdominal wall called a stoma that the bowel empties into. And then the lower part of the bowel, that empties down into the rectum eventually, that lower part of the small bowel was also brought out into a separate -- through a separate hole in the abdominal wall. So [Baby J] had two small holes in her abdominal wall through which her bowel was slightly protruding and those are called stomas.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Was the surgical plan to eventually rejoin those divided ends of the bowel?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, after a few months, I believe.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If we could go, please, to tile 11, Mr Murphy, which informs us of [Baby J]'s return to Chester, which occurred on Tuesday, 10 November 2015, so therefore now at 11 days old and having spent most of her short life to date at Alder Hey.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: On her return to Chester, what was the feeding regime in place for [Baby J]; do you recall?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. Initially, [Baby J] was receiving her feed intravenously, so that was total parenteral nutrition, TPN. But the plan was to gradually increase the amount of milk feeding into her tummy through a nasogastric tube. But that food, instead of going through the entire length of the bowel and coming out at the anus as usual, would come out the -- it's called the proximal stoma, the stoma nearest the top end of the bowel. And that food was only partially digested, it hadn't gone all the way through the bowel, but it had been partially digested and partially absorbed into the bloodstream.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Because it was only partially digested -- and also that meant [Baby J] wouldn't have received full nutrition from that food -the plan from the surgeons was to actually re-feed [Baby J] with that partially digested food as well as with more milk feeds. So it was called recycling of the feeds.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you for that explanation. At this point in time, 10 November, on her return on Chester, what was the respiratory position for [Baby J]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: As far as I'm aware, she had no respiratory problems.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: How was her progress upon return?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: [Baby J] made steady and acceptable, encouraging progress in that the amount of milk feeds she received was steadily increased. The amount of TPN was reduced until it could be stopped altogether. And then she was only receiving milk feeds. Those milk feeds were from her mother, her mother's expressed breast milk, topped up where necessary by some donor breast milk, and it was all initially given through a nasogastric tube into [Baby J]'s tummy, but increasingly [Baby J] was able to take the breast milk feed through a bottle, she could suck it herself. So steadily, the amount of milk given to [Baby J] increased by bottles and decreased through the nasogastric tube until she could actually manage all bottles.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Over the next 2 weeks or more, did she remain stable?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, she did. By the end of those 2.5 weeks or so she'd managed to transfer completely to bottle feeding, just managed that by that 2.5 weeks, remaining fine without any respiratory complications.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. What about the stoma? Did that cause any difficulties in this period of time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It was a challenge managing [Baby J]'s stoma and the stoma was mainly managed by her nurses, the feeding regime, because we rarely have babies on our unit in Chester with a stoma needing recycling feeds. But because of that we had been advised by the specialist regional surgical team in Liverpool how to manage the feeds and we were invited -- either nurses could contact the nurses at the neonatal surgical unit in Liverpool or we doctors could contact the surgeons for advice on managing the stomas.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: One of the problems experienced was that the stoma that was being used to recycle the feeds did become abrased, sort of bruised from time to time. It bled a little occasionally and even developed a small hole in the wall of the stoma. But all of that was discussed with the neonatal surgical team in Liverpool, who were satisfied with her progress.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Could you expand or clarify the small hole in the stoma that you have referred to? Can you explain that to us?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Part of the wall of the stoma had broken down and there was a small hole linking the edge of the wall deeper into the intestine. It's called a fistula. But the surgeons weren't concerned because their plan was to unattach the stomas, tidy up the ends, which they always do, cut off the ends, and then join the two bits back together. So the fact the stomas were getting a little bit bruised from the constant treatment, touching them
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: and recycling the feeds didn't concern the surgeons as long as the bleeding wasn't excessive, and it never was, because they were going to remove those ends of bowels to reattach the bowel.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And these manifestations, the small amount of bleeding, the ulcer, the fistula (inaudible: coughing) considered exceptional to [Baby J] from the perspective of the Alder Hey surgical team?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No. And we had to be guided by their advice because they deal with babies with stomas fairly frequently.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: (inaudible: coughing) move then, please, to the events of the 26th and 27 November.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: At that point in time were you the consultant paediatrician on call covering the neonatal unit?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, I was on call overnight, the 26th to 27 November 2015.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Prior to that, had you had any direct involvement with [Baby J]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Not that I can recall, no -- and not that seems to have been recorded in the notes either.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. If we go, please, to tile 165. We see some clinical notes created by a junior colleague of yours, Dr Verghese. Dr Verghese will join us tomorrow. It was not possible to have him here today to deal with these things in a strictly chronological order.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: These notes of events at 05.15 on the morning of 27 November, did you appraise yourself of the contents of these notes when a little later you attended upon [Baby J]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. Now, I can't remember now whether I read these notes when I saw [Baby J] a couple of hours later or whether I was told about these events. But I was aware that these events had taken place when I saw [Baby J] 2 hours later.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: In summary, to help us understand the big picture, what was the nature of the information that was either provided to you orally or read in these notes?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That [Baby J] had been very stable, as she had been for weeks beforehand, until she suddenly dropped her oxygen levels on two occasions, a little bit before and a little bit after 5 o'clock in the morning, I think.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And at that point in time, immediately prior to the sudden drops in oxygen levels, was she breathing in air, normally?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, she was breathing normally by herself in air.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: How was the drop in blood oxygen level noted?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: She had an oxygen saturation meter attached that had presumably had alarmed, but I wasn't there at that time.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We can see from Dr Verghese's note that on the first occasion, according to his record, the oxygen level dropped to 30%, and on the second occasion to 50%. How significant a drop in oxygen levels is that, Dr Gibbs?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Those are very significant drops. The manufacturers -and there's different manufacturers of different oxygen saturation meters, but mostly they will claim that when an oxygen saturation meter drops to about 70% or below, it's no longer reliable. It does mean it's very low, but the difference between 30% and 40% is difficult to gauge. Anything below 70% is very low and alarmingly low, but the actual reading is no longer reliable below 70% on most machines.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I'm grateful.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is that literally alarmingly low? In other words, the alarm goes off?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It's both. Both, my Lord, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What assistance was provided to [Baby J] in response to these drops?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: She needed to be supported with her breathing, given oxygen through a Neopuff device.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We will hear from Dr Verghese tomorrow, I anticipate.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We note that the first "profound desat" occurred when she was being handled during stoma care of some kind?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Stoma cares" it looks like, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: (Inaudible: no microphone). Thank you. But the second occurred at a point in time when she was not being handled?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's what Dr Verghese has recorded, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What's the potential significance and why is it noteworthy whether or not the baby was being handled?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm not sure because just being handled through stoma care should not cause oxygenation levels to drop in any case. So it's unclear why [Baby J]'s oxygenation level had dropped. If [Baby J] had been a premature baby with significant lung disease who was needing respiratory support and was needing extra oxygen, then sometimes just handling as part of normal care might cause a drop in oxygen levels. But [Baby J] was a little baby managing in air, without respiratory difficulties, so even though she first desaturated, dropped her oxygen, while her stoma care was taking place, it's still unclear why that should have precipitated a drop in oxygen level, but the second time it seemed to happen spontaneously. But neither is properly explained from what Dr Verghese has written.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: This is of course now 27 November. She had been alive for 27 days and some hours. And for almost all of that time, the stomas had been in place. How frequently would a stoma care regime require handling to provide stoma care?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Because of the recycling feeds, I think several times a day. I must confess the nursing staff would know better because they undertook that stoma care, but frequently is the simple answer -- and every day.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Could we go to tile 182, please, Mr Murphy, which records your swipe data entry at 06.34 on the 27th. Was that your arrival at the unit in response to a call or was that as part of your daily routine, as it were?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It's not part of my daily routine at 6.30 in the morning, no. I can't remember why I was on the unit at that time, but it wasn't for [Baby J] as far as I recall.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: It must have been for another baby. I haven't had the opportunity to look at the notes of all the babies that are on the unit that night and to review them to try to determine why I was there at that time.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. But you're sure that it wasn't to attend upon [Baby J]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Not as far as I can remember, no.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: From reminding yourself of the notes, did [Baby J] remain stable in the two or so hours after the events that Dr Verghese recorded at 05.50?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: As far as the notes record, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If we could please go to tile 196, which records the time, at 06.56, of a recorded event involving [Baby J], that is a clinical event. At the next tile we'll see your clinical notes. Before looking at them, can you share with us your recollections of these events?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: My recollection is mainly from having reviewed the notes. But [Baby J] again dropped her oxygenation level, but this time also dropped her heart rate, whereas the first time -- on the first two occasions Dr Verghese had attended earlier in the night she had dropped her oxygen levels alarmingly, but not dropped her heart rate much.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: This time she dropped both her oxygen levels and her heart rate and was needing support from the nurses.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Now, I can't recall whether it was the nurses who called me over to [Baby J] or whether the alarm was going off from her oxygen saturation meter that alerted me to the problem. But I wasn't with [Baby J] when she first dropped her oxygen saturation level, but I came and assisted the nurses who were with her.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Before we go to the detail, can you assist us to better understand the significance of a drop in heart rate together with a drop in oxygen saturation levels?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, either is of concern and can cause serious problems to a baby if not addressed, but both occurring together is more concern than just one occurring by itself. There's uncertainty about one which comes first: a drop in oxygen level can lead to a drop in heart rate level, but a drop in heart rate level conversely can cause the oxygen level to drop. These had both dropped pretty quickly together as far as, I think, the nurses looking after her were concerned, but the nurses looking after her would need to answer that.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Can we click on to tile 197, please, and bring up Dr Gibbs' notes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: 07.35, is that the time of the writing of the note?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, this is after the two events.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Which you have timed. Help us with that first sentence, please, if you would.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I wrote at 07.35 that there'd been two further episodes of sudden desats, that's dropping the oxygen level, and then in brackets "to unrecordable levels" -- the first one was at 06.56, so 4 minutes to 7, and then the second one was about 28 minutes
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: later 07.24. I put "plus bradycardia", so that means [Baby J] dropped her heart rate as well as her oxygen levels.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. You informed us a little earlier this morning about the unreliability of saturation levels below a certain threshold. Can you expand, please, upon the fact that her sudden desats fell to unrecordable levels?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: This just means it was well below 70%. When I say unreliable, the oxygen levels are still reliable in that they are abnormally very low but the exact level isn't meant to be reliable once it drops below 70%. The machines are definitely detecting a very low -- a worryingly low level of oxygen.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: On both of these occasions, as you indicated earlier, combined with bradycardia?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Your next sentence, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Both associated with clenching of hands, stiff limbs (upper greater than lower) and, on the second occasion, eyes deviated to the left."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Can you explain the significance of those observations, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: This is describing a seizure that [Baby J] was displaying, two seizures. She displayed it with each of the episodes, the one at just before 7 o'clock and the one at 7.24. Her limbs were stiff, abnormally stiff, and her hands were clenched. It was on the second occasion that the eyes deviated to one side, which is a sign of a seizure, particularly in neonatal babies.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: (Inaudible: no microphone) it's my fault, I have led you to deal with these events almost as one. Let's break them up and deal with them chronologically so that we get the full narrative history here.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You were on the unit at the time of the first of these episodes --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. But I wasn't with [Baby J] as far as I recall.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You were not with [Baby J] but you do recall going to [Baby J] but you can't recall whether that was in response to a verbal request from a nurse or in response to the sound of the monitoring alarms?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct. But more likely someone had called for help.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And what was happening when you first arrived at [Baby J]'s cot side?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, her oxygen levels were low, but as I say, unrecordably low. The most notable thing with [Baby J] she was abnormally stiff with all her limbs held out stiffly and hands clenched. She was being given respiratory support with a Neopuff. I can't remember who was giving that, though. It wasn't me and I was arriving at that time.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Can you remember which members of staff were at [Baby J]'s cot side at this point?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, partly my memory is refreshed by reviewing the notes, and it was Staff Nurse Griffith and Staff Nurse Letby.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Did you immediately provide assistance?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What did you do? What assistance did you give?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I can't remember exactly what I did and it doesn't say here what I did. Fortunately, [Baby J] did not need cardiac compressions, so her heart rate must have been improving and she didn't need any medication immediately at that stage. So I was observing her and trying to determine what had happened to cause her to drop her oxygen levels and then develop a seizure.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: For the sake of clarity, could you describe the manifestations of the seizure, the symptoms displayed during the first of the two episodes?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: [Baby J]'s four limbs being stiffly extended with her hands clenched, so fisting her hands.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What is that indicative of?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, she's displaying a seizure.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And how did you respond to that display?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, fortunately it began to resolve. After about -- I've recorded here after about 10 minutes, which is a reasonably long seizure.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Looking at your note, the stiffness took 10 minutes to settle on the first occasion?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Let's stay with the first occasion. So after about 10 minutes and a passing of the stiffness, what if any care or treatment did you provide to [Baby J] at this point in time? We're now about 7.06 or thereabouts.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Right. She was still requiring the Neopuff respiratory support. I don't think I'd taken it over on this first occasion, one of the nurses was still giving her respiratory support. But the concern then was to investigate why she'd had this seizure and why she'd dropped her oxygen levels.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And as to the duration of the respiratory support, if we look further down in your next note, does it read:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Needed Neopuff ventilation for 20 minutes on the first occasion"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. I think one of the nurses recorded 16 minutes, but somewhere between 16 and 20 minutes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. And your next note describes the perfusion?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. During that first episode, while she was having her seizure, the perfusion was poor and that would have meant she was pale. I haven't recorded any more details than that. So she was given 20ml per kilogram, which for her weight then would have been about 30-35ml, of saline intravenously to improve her circulation.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Did it appear to have a positive effect?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Did that effectively conclude the first episode or are there any other features about that first episode that you regard as important?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No, it had stopped. The seizure had stopped after about 10 minutes, providing [Baby J] was -- assisted ventilation with a Neopuff continued for about another 6 to 10 minutes after that. But by that stage her circulation was back to normal and she was breathing again by herself and her oxygen levels had returned back to normal, well above 90%. But there wasn't too much time before the second event happened.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And in between events, did you remain with [Baby J] or did you attend to some other responsibilities or can't you recall?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That I'm afraid I can't recall. But it is important because if I was still with [Baby J] then I was with her at the time the second event started. I wasn't there when the first event started, which is why I have tried to remember whether I was still with her and I can't remember that.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I think it more likely than not that I had moved away from her briefly because having suffered a seizure, there are various conditions that can cause a seizure that we could rule out quite quickly on [Baby J]. It depended what her recent blood tests had shown. I think it's likely that I'd gone look at her results, which are on the computers but not inside the outside nursery rooms. So I think I probably was looking at results on the computer in between these two episodes, but I was close by to [Baby J]'s nursery at that time. I may have gone to talk to Dr Verghese as well. But I didn't record that in the notes and I can't remember. But events quickly moved on to the second event.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. We'll return to the blood results a little later. Let's go to the second event now, which your note here times at 07.24 hours.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Tell us about that, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, again, [Baby J] dropped her oxygen level and her heart rate and needed support with her breathing, just as in the first episode, less than half an hour earlier.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Now, I had helped to give her the Neopuff ventilation for that second episode, which is why I would have been nearby, but as I've said, I cannot remember whether I was still with her when it began. I think more likely than not I wasn't, but I can't be sure. I supported her with the breathing.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Her circulation did not deteriorate as it had on the first occasion, so she didn't need any more intravenous fluid, and the episode was much shorter. She did display again stiffness of all her limbs, clenching of her hands, but on this second occasion her eyes deviated towards the left. That was all part of a seizure but it stopped after 3 or 4 minutes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Just to break that down, is it your evidence that you recall Neopuffing [Baby J] during this episode and from that memory you conclude that you must have been close at hand when it began?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. When I say I recall, I'm recorded in the notes as giving the Neopuff. And I cannot remember whether I was with her when this episode started or whether I was nearby.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's go to your note then. So (inaudible: no microphone) times the duration of the stiffness, we've looked at
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: episode 1, 10 minutes to settle and you noted 3 to 4 minutes on the second occasion?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Your note tells us how long she required ventilation for on the first occasion. What about the second?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Five minutes on the second occasion, so much shorter.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Her perfusion on the second occasion?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It was likely to have been normal because she didn't require any intervention. But I can't remember now back 7 years ago exactly what her perfusion was like, except I've recorded that her perfusion was fine after these two episodes had finished. So after the second episode, her perfusion was normal.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: As with the first episode, was there bradycardia evident at this point?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I think -- it was recorded. I can't remember now seeing the number myself of the heart rate.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Turn to the note. Towards the middle of your note there's a sentence that begins with the words "air entry equal".
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So air entry was equal, so listening in to [Baby J]'s chest there was air entry equal on either side and her abdomen was not distended. Shall I continue?
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Post each episode [so after each episode] perfusion satisfactory."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And I describe how I tell that because her capillary refill time was 1 to 2 seconds, which means normal circulation. And even more so, I put it in brackets underneath that, central and peripheral, because you can check a central circulation by pressing on the chest or the centre part of the body and yet you might still have some reduced circulation only manifest if you press on a peripheral part of the body like the hand or foot.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But I say here the circulation was fine because both central and peripheral capillary refill times were normal. But that's after both episodes had finished and she'd needed -- [Baby J] had needed some saline bolus of fluid during the first episode.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Why did you consider it important to gauge her circulation through that method?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, firstly to see if she'd recovered from these two episodes, but secondly, there are a lot of causes why the oxygen level might drop. There are various causes why a baby may exhibit a seizure and some of those are associated with very poor perfusion. So not enough blood getting to the brain can lead to a seizure. But in [Baby J] her perfusion had recovered by the end of these two episodes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thus did you rule out that as the potential cause of these seizures in this baby?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I couldn't say ruled out but it seemed quite unlikely.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's return to your note. In the subparagraph that begins "blood glucose"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, that's an abbreviation for blood. Blood glucose 9.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That's moderately high. The blood glucose level should normally be roughly between 4 and 7. When someone is stressed that does tend to push up the blood sugar level so the fact this level was slightly high is -- it's likely that [Baby J] had been stressed, which is exactly what you'd expect if she had just had two seizures. The importance of the blood sugar level being high is a very low blood sugar level can cause a seizure, but the fact the level was 9 during the second episode meant it was very unlikely to have been low around that time, so was not the cause of the seizure.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Could you take us through your next entry and the significance of it, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Right. The line begins:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "NB [which means 'note well'] the electrolytes were normal on the ABG [an abbreviation for blood gas] earlier in the night."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I do comment although the potassium level, the K+ is potassium level, was 3, that's lower end, just below the lower end of normal for potassium.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I also mention that the calcium level -- the Ca2+ is the calcium level -- had been normal on the bloods taken 3 days earlier or
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: 2.5 days earlier, 24/11/15. The significance of this is that a very low blood sodium level or a very low blood calcium level can cause seizures and that does happen in babies for various reasons. It's not common.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But here we were looking for reasons why [Baby J] had displayed these two seizures that I'd witnessed and the seizures were not explained by a low blood glucose, because it wasn't low, nor were her seizures explained by abnormal electrolyte levels because they weren't abnormal. The potassium being a little low does not cause seizures.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Are these the blood results that you told us about earlier that you at some point checked?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: While we're on that topic, can we go to tile 200, please (inaudible: no microphone) document there. Have you endorsed any part of that document?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. I've written that prescription there.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You say that prescription singular. There seem to be two separate endorsements there; do you agree?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, but the bottom one is crossed out, so I don't know if it was given.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Look at the times to the right of the document, the times when they were started. The upper endorsement seems to be 07.20 and the lower one at 07.09.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. That's correct. I'm just a little confused why they're given in reverse order, but anyway, the bottom one is the saline. So the NaCl is the saline, sodium chloride. This was the bolus that was given during that first seizure. I mentioned in my notes earlier, it's 20ml per kilogram and I estimated that was about 30-35ml, it's not, it was 38ml from [Baby J]'s weight at that time. The nurses record it was given at 07.09.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So although a line has been (inaudible: no microphone) dashed through that endorsement, you recall, do you, and your clinical notes confirm, that that bolus of saline was given?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, and it's signed for by the nurses who had given it.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Well, I think it would be helpful to know what is on that form when you -- what is your writing and the timing of your writing compared to the other writing.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Taking the first entry, the 10% glucose, you initially wrote, it seems, 11.9 volume, put a line through that. Then the rate/duration -- 11.9ml per hour is that?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Going along to the right, route, IV, intravenous?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That's your signature, is it?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What happens thereafter? The next column is to the right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Nurses then administer the fluid and they sign for it when they administer it. Those columns to the right, "given by" and "time and date started", are filled in by the nursing staff.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So you have no part in that?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No, I didn't fill that in.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And then below, the next entry, same again, is it --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: -- up to your signature under the "prescribed by" --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Exactly. I'd prescribed it. The nurses have then signed for it. In fact, the nurse's signature is Staff Nurse Griffith for both of those.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: (Inaudible: no microphone) the route and your signature appears to be dashed out there.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Did you do that?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I can't remember. But the -- looking at the width of the line, it looks like the same pen that had written the prescription, so likely me.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But was it prescribed?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It was prescribed and it was given because it's signed for by the nurses with the time it was given during that first seizure.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Can you explain why in those circumstances then the record has been crossed through?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No, I can't remember why I would have crossed it through, but one possible reason is that it wouldn't be given again because that 10% glucose above it is to be given continuously. So to make sure the saline wasn't given repeatedly, it has been crossed through, probably after it had been given.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: To avoid a reader taking that as an instruction --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: -- to repeat?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, because this is an infusion chart, so these are fluids that are constantly running in a baby and that was just a one-off saline, which is probably why I crossed it out after it had been given. If it had been crossed out before it had been given, it shouldn't have been given.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And it was (inaudible: no microphone)?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It was given, yes. The glucose was because after these two seizures, the decision was. While we investigated [Baby J] for the cause of her seizures and treated her for possible causes, that she shouldn't be fed by milk into her tummy until we were sure that she was settled and fully recovered, so instead she was treated -- given nutrition with glucose running constantly at 11.9ml an hour.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Could we return to Dr Gibbs' note, which was housed amongst other places behind tile 197, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We'd reached the point where you recorded the blood glucose, et cetera --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: -- checked on the electrolytes et cetera and an earlier blood test results. Then you moved to the impression --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: -- that had been left with you. You've more than once told us that it appeared to be a pair of seizures.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And that's the simple note you've made there.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's right, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Was that an impression made by the stiffness of the limbs, the eyes (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Was there any record of [Baby J] ever having presented with seizures prior to this pair of events?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Not that I was aware of and not that I can find reviewing her medical notes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What, if any, treatment did you prescribe to address the seizures at this point in time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, several treatments. Because the important aim for [Baby J] was to try and determine why she had had that seizure. That's why in the next line down it's "[query] septic": had infection caused her to suddenly deteriorate and cause her to have seizures? And the main infection that causes seizures is meningitis, but when young babies develop infection anywhere in the body, it can spread rapidly into the bloodstream, which is septicaemia, and rapidly into the brain. So infection(?) can be associated with meningitis as well as infection elsewhere in the body.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So I was wondering whether infection had caused her seizure.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We glanced at Dr Verghese's note and we will look at it in more detail with Dr Verghese, but as a matter of fact had Dr Verghese started antibiotics?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm not sure. I thought he had but looking through the notes, his intention was to start antibiotics after the first two desaturation episodes because in young babies who are showing -- misbehaving in any way, so showing (sic) concern -and particularly dropping oxygen level is causing concern -- we have to think, could infection be causing this?
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The test for infection means looking at the white cell count in the blood, looking at the C-reactive protein, the CRP, in the blood and taking blood cultures but those results are often only available over the next few days. Blood cultures take a few days to be processed in the laboratory to know if bacteria are growing. Often, the white cell count and the CRP only rise over the few days after the infection has started, not before or at
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: the beginning of an infection. So it takes -- it's a retrospective diagnosis often. But we can't wait for those tests before treating, which is why we have to give antibiotics early.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I think Dr Verghese had started antibiotics, but I said he needed -- [Baby J] needed antibiotics as well so I'm not sure whether I changed the antibiotics or whether this was the first time antibiotics were given to [Baby J] that night.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We can see the antibiotics that you prescribed as part of that plan. Was that to cover a wide range of organisms?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, including meningitis; that's the cefotaxime and teicoplanin.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We digressed a little. What is it that you prescribed to address the seizures?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I am sorry for not answering that straightaway, but you're right, trying to treat the infection is treating the seizures as well. But a very specific treatment for seizures we gave to [Baby J] -- I decided [Baby J] needed was phenobarbitone, an anticonvulsant medication.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That's because she'd had two seizures in a short space of time, so to prevent her continue to have repeated seizures affecting her oxygen levels and breathing.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You have told us that on your reading of her notes she had never presented with seizures prior to this morning.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What about post 27 November? Did [Baby J] ever present with seizures again?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No. She had no convulsive -- this was a convulsive seizure or stiffening seizure that she exhibited this night. She never had it again to my knowledge and I followed [Baby J] up in clinic after she'd left the neonatal unit until she was 19 months old. I can't say after 19 months whether she's ever had any seizures.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I ought to add though, when we were following up in clinic, at around a year of age, her parents had reported she was showing brief blanking episodes, but those were very likely to have been inattention episodes and not any form of epilepsy. There is a childhood form of epilepsy that just manifests by blanking episodes, but [Baby J] had inattention, not blanking epilepsy, at about a year of age.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So the phenobarbitone that was prescribed to address these convulsive seizures at this point in time, was that
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: provided to [Baby J] on a continuing basis or just on 27 November?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It was just given on 27 November. The initial dose of phenobarbitone lasts 12 to 24 hours and should prevent further seizures. Other colleagues of mine looking after [Baby J] after that, because she'd been so stable and settled so well after these episodes, decided not to continue the phenobarbitone, although they would have done if she then developed further seizures, but she didn't have any further seizures.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So whatever caused the seizures on 27 November did not return?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But you can't be certain as to what was the cause of the seizures?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No. We were looking for rare causes. Along that list of the plan at the bottom is ultrasound of the head and that's just in case [Baby J] had suffered a bleed in her head. Premature babies can suffer cerebral bleeds usually in the first few week of life, the first few days. [Baby J] was now a month old so unlikely at this stage, but she had the ultrasound scan and in fact all these investigations did not reveal any cause for her seizures.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We'll return to the seizures shortly, but absent from this plan is any, it would seem, suggested intubation or mechanical ventilation. Did you consider that?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It always needs -- yes, I must have considered it. It always needs considering when a child has needed support for their ventilation and whilst I had been in attendance with [Baby J] she'd needed Neopuffing twice, 20 minutes the first time roughly, 5 minutes roughly the second time. But she recovered so well afterwards and was so stable, in fact was in air afterwards, not needing any additional oxygen, that I didn't feel that she needed to be intubated and provided with continuing ventilation.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: My Lord, I estimate I'll be about another 10 or 15 minutes with Dr Gibbs.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: We'll break off there because I'm sure that Mr Myers will have questions anyway. It's a little bit later than normal, 1.05, so we'll break off until 2.05, please, members of the jury.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the absence of the jury)
You're very familiar with your obligations, Dr Gibbs, as a witness. 2.05. Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The short adjournment)

Dr Gibbs, before lunch you told us about two episodes of sudden deterioration at 06.56 and 07.24 on 27 November 2015, which were characterised by marked drops in blood oxygen level and heart rate and the exhibiting of the signs of a seizure or fit.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What, if any, investigations did you undertake or cause to be undertaken to try and discover the cause of these seizures?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, the blood sugar level was checked during the second seizure and was found to be high, whereas a very low blood sugar can cause seizures, so that wasn't the cause. The electrolytes, having been checked recently, were normal. They were checked later on in the day and were found to still be normal.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: As I've mentioned, it's not possible to know immediately whether a baby is infected, but it's important to treat for possible infection, so those tests for infection were undertaken and treatment was started for infection.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Then it was planned to undertake a brain scan just in case, a relatively unlikely possibility, [Baby J] had suffered from a haemorrhage or other problem in her brain causing her seizure.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Also the plan was to X-ray [Baby J]'s tummy to see if that showed any changes or any concern -- and having stomas, having a bowel perforation, like [Baby J] had had at the beginning of her life, in themselves do not cause seizures, but if there had been a complication giving rise to infection, like peritonitis or infection spreading elsewhere, as I said before an infection, particularly if it spreads to the brain, can cause seizures, which is why, indirectly, it was important to investigate her bowel condition.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Mr Murphy, can you take us to tile 170, please? It records the collection of a pathology specimen at 06.09 on 27
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: November 2015. If we can click on to the underlying document, please. What does this record, Dr Gibbs?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It shows that the specimen collected at the time, as you say, after 5 days showed no bacterial growth. That blood sample, it says:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Blood culture central line."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So it was taken out of a central line that [Baby J] had -- I don't know if the central line has been discussed in court.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We've watched an animation this morning of a Broviac line.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, she had a Broviac line in and that's where the sample was taken from. Given the timing of the specimen, it was before the two seizures that I saw so this investigation must have been arranged by Dr Verghese after the two episodes he had witnessed.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you for that. Could we go to tile 171 or the document that underpins it, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Can you help us with this, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Right. This is a blood specimen result and it was collected on that same night, 27/11/15, and again at the same time, it's recorded as having been collected, that's at 06.09, so prior -- just under an hour prior to the two seizures that I witnessed, but maybe about an hour after the two episodes Dr Verghese had recorded.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If you look down the left-hand side, ordered, it shows U&Es, LFTs, calcium profile, CRP, full blood count. Those were the tests that were requested and then in the long columns are the results of those tests.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And which, if any (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Of note, the one at the top, a sodium of 138, that's normal, because a very low sodium is well below 130 can cause seizures, but that wasn't the cause of her seizures.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The calcium level, about five down, six down, is 2.29, within the normal range.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The CRP level, halfway down the list, is less than 1, but it's important to repeat that over the next day or two because this is a sign of infection or possible infection if it rises well above 10 and it can take a day or two to rise. So at this stage
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: it wasn't elevated and indeed it didn't rise over the next couple of days looking at [Baby J]'s notes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Her full blood count there, the WBC, is also normal at 8.1 and again it did not rise over the next few days suggesting there was no infection causing [Baby J]'s seizures.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: For the sake of completeness if we could go to tile 351, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sorry, just before we leave this tile, just below the arrow now, the second one down, Hb is the haemoglobin level. It is rather low at 78. Indeed, I believe -- I wasn't involved then -- later on in that day it was decided to give [Baby J] a blood transfusion.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What, (inaudible: no microphone) context of investigating (inaudible) cause of seizures what's the significance of that low count?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The low haemoglobin would not be a cause of seizures no.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Can we go to tile 351 then? This takes us to a specimen collected at 16.00 on 28 November, the following day. Is that of any significance here?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It's called a central line site swab. It shows some bacteria called Klebsiella, but that's on the outside of the Broviac line. That isn't significant at this stage.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If a Broviac line consistently shows bacteria there's a chance those bacteria may spread down the line and into the bloodstream. But the way the line is inserted, and you say you have seen a video, the surgeons tunnel the line under the skin for quite a few centimetres before it comes out of the neck or chest wall. And the idea that tunnelling is to try and prevent bacteria moving along the line into the bloodstream. It would only be significant if this bacteria had been found in [Baby J]'s blood and you would have expected a high CRP and white cell count in association with that. So this isn't anything related to the cause of her seizures.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. So blood tests were undertaken as part of an investigation into the cause of the seizure and yielded no indicators?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: There was an abdominal ultrasound; is that right?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct, later on, during the day of the 27th and that was normal.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And that was an investigation into whether there was a further perforation of the bowel --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Perforation or an abscess having collected in the abdomen but none was seen.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The seizures -- she exhibited signs of seizure at the time of the sudden deteriorations. Might there be a causal relationship between deteriorations and the seizure?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. It is a chicken-and-egg situation: did the seizure cause a deterioration, in other words if you develop a seizure it will affect your breathing. If you go stiff, as [Baby J] was, she was persistently stiff for several minutes on each occasion, that can drop the blood oxygen level. So the low blood oxygen may be a consequence of the seizure.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Against that in [Baby J]'s case is, so far as I can ascertain from the notes and as far as I can remember, the initiating concern was the drop in oxygen. So the oxygen drop happened very early on, not after the seizure had started.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And also, having not found any cause for the seizure, it's less likely the seizure led to the oxygen drop but more likely, having found no other cause for the seizure, that a lack of oxygen to the brain had actually caused the seizure.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So the oxygen drop could, and you think probably did, cause the seizure?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's a distinct possibility since we found no other cause but we certainly documented very low oxygen levels in [Baby J] associated with a seizure.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And were you able to identify the cause of the oxygen drop?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No, because up until then [Baby J] had had no breathing difficulties -- well, in the preceding few weeks.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And what about post 27 November?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I believe over the next few weeks, and certainly the following days, she had no breathing difficulties.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Things changed a little 2.5 weeks later but I wasn't involved then and others would presumably be able to provide information to the court about the episode a couple of weeks later.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: (Inaudible) referring to December 2015 --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: -- which resulted in [Baby J] being moved to Manchester?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. But after the two seizures I witnessed on the night of the 27th, up until that episode, that deterioration 2.5 weeks later, [Baby J] had no breathing difficulties as far as I recall.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You mentioned earlier that notwithstanding the fact that she was moved to Manchester and ultimately Alder Hey, she did return to your care as part of your paediatric outpatient clinic; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: It's a matter of record and I'm not sure it's not controversial, did you see her four times between April 2016 and June 2017?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: She attended my clinic four times and I saw her on three of those occasions.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Having considered the notes from those visits and the letters that you dictated, how had she progressed by that stage?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: She was managing very well. She was growing well at that stage and developing normally.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: There was, I think you told us earlier, some sensitivity to cow's milk; is that right?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. All the time she was on the neonatal unit -- I'm not sure at the very end when she had moved to Manchester Children's and then Alder Hey, but most of the time at the Countess of Chester she was taking her mother's breast milk.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: When she then transferred to cow's milk, which is probably after she had gone home, but I'm not sure. At some stage she swapped to cow's milk and became sensitive to it and actually briefly attended at the Countess of Chester with blood in her stool, thought to be due to sensitivity to cow's milk protein, so she had to have a low allergy milk.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Was that problem effectively managed?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. Most children grow out of it, but it takes a few years to grow out of cow's milk intolerance.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: When considering [Baby J] as an outpatient, what about the bowel perforation and any consequences thereof, how did that progress?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The only abnormality related to her bowel that I could notice, both from my examination and from talking to her parents, was the fact she had a prominent scar on her abdomen. Otherwise she was managing very well with her bowels. The fact she was growing well was a good indication her bowels were functioning well.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Ultimately, did you discharge her as an outpatient when she was approximately 19 months old?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And at that stage was she a well little girl?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Could you remain there, please?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
I want to ask you first about the two incidents recorded in the clinical notes at 05.15, the first two incidents. Are you clear about what I am referring to?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, the one Dr Verghese recorded.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That's right, yes. In fact, just so there can be no doubt, could we put up tile 165, please? Pop behind that and we can be clear what it says.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We have two profound desaturations recorded in the note made at 05.15; do you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: From your assessment of the notes and the clinical history, [Baby J] appears to have been doing well before these incidents?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And you've looked at her breathing and you've looked at her weight and you haven't identified any complication that was playing a part in her condition prior to this; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: As far as the weight is concerned, [Baby J] was gaining weight relatively slowly. But we had addressed that by increasing the volume of her feeds and adding fortifier, a sort of calorie supplement, to her feed. That's not surprising in a baby who had her bowel problems and was having this recycling of feeds.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: She appears to have been stable before this happened?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, but gaining weight slowly.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Gaining weight slowly. And certainly to you it was unclear why this should have happened; is that fair to say?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: As a general matter, is it possible for there to be a sudden desaturation like the one or the ones we're looking at here if an infection is developing?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That can be one way that a baby presents with infection, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Although, so there's no misunderstanding, your assessment of the evidence is that there's no particular sign of any infection that was identified afterwards; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct but, as I think I mentioned, both Dr Verghese and then later myself began treatment for [Baby J] for infection in case there might have been infection. So we were not certain that night that she wasn't developing an infection. Subsequent tests and the passage of time told us she didn't have an infection.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If a baby is treated with antibiotics for infection very rapidly, might that mean that subsequently no signs of infection are apparent?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: As far as I am aware, that's very unusual. Antibiotics don't work instantly, they take several days to have a full effect, even when you have chosen the correct antibiotic, which is partly guesswork, but educated guesswork, for what you think might be causing the infection. You would still expect a significant rise in the CRP blood level and in the white cell count.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So if we discount infection, then these desaturations remain unexplained so far as you can determine?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I'm going to ask you now just about the part of the event involving [Baby J] where you were on the unit, round about or just shortly before 7 o'clock.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You have told us the nursing staff you recall being present when you attended the first one of the incidents, the second pair of incidents.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I've had to rely on the notes to be sure who was there.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I first did the statement on [Baby J] 3 years after this event and I couldn't remember all the details myself.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: No, well, no one is expecting you to remember all the details going back that far. You remember Nurse Griffith; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And you remember Nurse Letby?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Do you remember Nurse Dennison also being present at some point?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: She was around then, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: All right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And at that stage [Baby J] was in the outside nurseries where the nursery nurses like Nurse Dennison cared for the babies there.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right. When [Baby J] had the final deterioration, what you might think of as the fourth in the course of that morning, so we have two that we have seen on Dr Verghese's note and then the two we've seen on your note, we see that you were involved in providing Neopuff --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: -- to [Baby J], don't we? And just so we can be quite clear, your recollection is you might have been in the nursery, you might not, you would have thought you probably would be typing up notes on the computer outside the nursery?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not typing, looking for results on the computer --
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: All right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: -- the results we've talked about, the calcium, the recent electrolytes and so on.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But involved in the computer outside the nursery?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I was nearby, but I can't remember if I was with [Baby J] or nearby when she had that fourth episode.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So in fairness that's something you can't be absolutely sure about one way or another?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: In dealing with the question of the seizures that you've described, the two times you were there, Dr Gibbs, can infection be a cause of seizure?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, but usually when it involves meningitis irritating the brain.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We notice in your note you have "[query] septic", haven't you, next to it when you look at the seizure?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, for any baby that deteriorates, sepsis is usually a possibility that has to be considered.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And you were asked the question about when you look at seizure and breathing difficulties which way round they go and I think you began by saying it's a slightly chicken-and-egg situation.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I suppose it's identifying the desaturations and the need for resuscitation overnight as well as identifying the seizures. But I do know that hypoxia, for example, can cause seizures if the brain becomes hypoxic. So that would be possibly the most likely cause for the seizures. But then it still remains a question why was [Baby J] hypoxic when for the 2 or 3 weeks beforehand she'd been breathing normally in air and there was no evidence of infection in the blood tests that we did or any of the investigations that we did to suggest any significant infection anywhere. blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So we've heard that infection can take a few days to become apparent --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: -- but nothing in the period thereafter?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Nothing subsequently became apparent in those days. We stopped antibiotics and she remained well, you know, for the weeks afterwards, really, until the next episode.

blocks.text: Mm-hm.

blocks.text: I'd seen her -- the 27th was a Friday and this was a Sunday. I was just summarising the problems. You mentioned necrotising enterocolitis as the diagnosis at the beginning. Strictly speaking, it wasn't typical of necrotising enterocolitis.

blocks.text: Right. Thank you for correcting me.

blocks.text: Too soon to be (overspeaking) feeds?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Exactly. So it was a problem from birth, a congenital problem with the gut that we talk about. So there was a necrotic section of bowel that was taken out. The necrosis was there but the enterocolitis wasn't there, it was -- sorry, just to correct you on that.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: It's my error and thank you for correcting it.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's okay. So I was just summarising the diagnoses and the sad twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome that [Baby J]'s twin suffered from and, sadly, didn't survive the pregnancy. Then I've described the abnormal movements and the deterioration on 27 November.

blocks.text: So that's very much a potted history of the concerns that --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: -- so far?
